verses.translation: And after{H310} this I saw{H7200} another{H312} messenger{H4397} descending{H3381} from the heavens{H8064}, and to him was strength{H3581} and great{H1419} might{H1369}, and the ground{H127} shone{H215} from his light{H216}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah, H127 — 'the ground') — NOT אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth'). Greek has ἡ γῆ ('the earth'). The Hebrew consistently uses adamah throughout ch. 18 (vv. 1, 23, 24), tying the imagery to the Genesis creation — the ground that was cursed (Gen 3:17), the ground from which man was formed (Gen 2:7). A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use ארץ, not adamah.

Uses כֹּחַ וּגְבוּרָה (koach ugvurah — 'strength and might') — the physical power pair. Greek: ἐξουσίαν μεγάλην ('great authority'). Hebrew describes raw physical/spiritual power; Greek describes institutional authority. A back-translator would use שלטון (shilton — 'authority'), not the koach/gevurah warrior-power pair.

Uses מֵאוֹרוֹ (me'oro — 'from his light', from or H216). Greek: ἐκ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ ('from his glory'). Hebrew: light radiates; Greek: glory radiates. Different qualities — Hebrew uses the elemental creation light (Gen 1:3); Greek uses a theological concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'strength and might' (physical power). Greek: 'great authority' (institutional power).
Hebrew: 'from his light.' Greek: 'from his glory.'
Hebrew: 'the ground' (adamah). Greek: 'the earth' (γῆ).
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') to preserve the Genesis creation connection, as in ch. 21:1.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 43:2 — 'and the earth (הארץ) shone from his glory.' The Hebrew Revelation echoes Ezekiel but substitutes adamah for erets and 'light' for 'glory' — a deliberate variation.

verses.translation: And he cried out{H6817} with all{H3605} his strength{H3581} and said{H559}: Fallen{H5307}, fallen{H5307} is the great{H1419} city{H5892} Bavel{H894}, and she has become a dwelling{H1754} of the adversaries and a hiding-place{H5641} for all{H3605} the impure{H2931} ones, of fowl{H5775} and creeping things{H8318}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 21:9: נָפְלָה נָפְלָה בָּבֶל ('fallen, fallen is Babylon'). Both Hebrew and Greek preserve the doubled verb, but the Hebrew preserves the exact Isaiah form.

CRITICAL: Uses הַשְּׂטָנִים (hasatanim — 'the adversaries/satans', H7854) — the Hebrew word שׂטן in its original sense of 'adversary/accuser' (Num 22:22, 1 Sam 29:4, 1 Ki 11:14,23, Job 1-2, Zech 3:1). Greek δαιμονίων ('demons') is an entirely different class of being. Hebrew satan = legal adversary/accuser; Greek daimon = spirit being. A back-translator from Greek 'demons' would use שדים (shedim — 'demons,' Deut 32:17, Ps 106:37), NOT satanim.

Uses שְׁרָצִים (sheratzim, H8318 — 'creeping things/swarming creatures') — the specific Levitical creation term from Genesis 1:20-21 and the unclean creatures list (Lev 11:29-31,41-43). Greek has no equivalent term. The Hebrew imports creation/Levitical unclean-animal vocabulary.

Uses לְהַסְתִּיר (lehistir — 'to hide/conceal', from satar H5641). Greek φυλακή means 'prison/guard.' Hebrew: Babylon becomes a HIDING-PLACE (where impure things conceal themselves); Greek: Babylon becomes a PRISON (where things are confined). Different imagery — concealment vs. captivity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'adversaries' (satanim). Greek: 'demons' (δαιμονίων). Different beings.
Hebrew: 'hiding-place.' Greek: 'prison.' Different concept.
Hebrew: 'creeping things' (sheratzim). Greek: no equivalent — adds 'every unclean and hated bird.'
translation_notes: 'Adversaries' for satanim preserves the Hebrew legal/accusatory meaning.
'Creeping things' for sheratzim — the Levitical unclean swarming creatures of Lev 11.
textual_notes: Isaiah 13:21-22 — 'wild beasts shall lie down there... and howling creatures shall fill her houses.' The desolation of Babylon with unclean creatures is an Isaianic image.

verses.translation: For all{H3605} drank{H8354} from her wine{H3196}, and the kings{H4428} of the earth{H776} committed fornication{H2184} with her, and all{H3605} the merchants{H5503} grew rich from their great{H1419} desires{H8378}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תַּאֲוָתֵיהֶם (ta'avateihem — 'THEIR desires/lusts', H8378). Greek: τοῦ στρήνους αὐτῆς ('HER luxury/excess'). Hebrew: the merchants grew rich from THEIR OWN lusts; Greek: they grew rich from HER luxury. Different possessor and different concept — Hebrew internal desire vs. Greek external luxury.

Uses סוֹחֲרִים (socharim — 'merchants', from sachar H5503 — 'to trade/go about'). This is the standard OT merchant word (Gen 23:16, 37:28, Isa 23:2, Ezek 27:21,36). The -im plural is natural Hebrew; the concept of itinerant traders is deeply embedded in the OT.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from their great desires.' Greek: 'from HER luxury.' Different possessor.
Hebrew: 'all drank' (subject unspecified). Greek: 'all the nations drank' — specifies 'nations.'

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} another{H312} voice{H6963} from the heavens{H8064} saying{H559}: Go out{H3318} from her, my people{H5971}, so that you not be punished with her on account of her iniquities{H5771}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT OT QUOTATION: צְאוּ מִמֶּנָּה עַמִּי ('Go out from her, my people') — echoes Jeremiah 51:45 (צְאוּ מִתּוֹכָהּ עַמִּי — 'Go out from her midst, my people') and Isaiah 52:11 (סוּרוּ סוּרוּ צְאוּ מִשָּׁם — 'Depart, depart, go out from there'). The imperative צְאוּ (tse'u — 'go out!') is the Exodus verb — the same command that launched Israel from Egypt. A back-translator from Greek ἐξέλθετε could arrive at tse'u, but the combination tse'u + ammi is the Jeremiah formula.

Uses עֲווֹנוֹתֶיהָ (avonoteiha — 'her iniquities', from avon H5771). Greek: ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις αὐτῆς ('her sins'). Hebrew avon is not merely 'sin' (חטא, chatat) — it is guilt-bearing iniquity, the accumulated weight of wrongdoing and its consequences (Gen 4:13, Ex 34:7, Isa 53:5-6). A back-translator from Greek ἁμαρτία would use חטאת (chatat — 'sin'), not the heavier avon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: one clause — 'so that you not be punished with her.' Greek splits into TWO: 'that you not share in her sins AND that you not receive from her plagues.' Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: תִּתְעַנְּשׁוּ (tit'anshu — 'you be punished') appears in brackets in the source, suggesting editorial restoration. This is a later Hebrew form.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:45 — 'Go out from her midst, my people (צאו מתוכה עמי)! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of YHWH!' The same command, same context — fleeing Babylon before divine judgment.

verses.translation: For her iniquities{H5771} have touched{H5060} the heavens{H8064}, and YHWH{H3068} shall remember{H2142} her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נָגַע (naga, H5060 — 'touched/reached/struck') — the Levitical contact verb used for touching impure things (Lev 5:2-3, 7:19,21, 11:24-39, Num 19:11). Her iniquities have made physical CONTACT with heaven — they have defiled the divine realm. Greek ἠκολούθησαν ('followed/accumulated') means merely that her sins piled up. A back-translator from Greek would use הגיעו (higi'u — 'reached/arrived'), not the Levitical contact verb naga.
Uses YHWH (H3068) — the covenant name. Greek: ὁ Θεός ('God'). Consistent pattern of Hebrew preserving the divine name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'touched the heavens' (physical contact). Greek: 'followed/accumulated up to heaven.' Different metaphor.
Hebrew: YHWH. Greek: God.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:9 — 'for her judgment reaches to the heavens (אל השמים) and is lifted up to the skies.' The same imagery of sin reaching heaven.

verses.translation: And as she did{H6213}, do{H6213} to her, and repay{H7999} her double{H3718} twofold according to her deeds{H4639}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּפֶל כִּפְלַיִם (kefel kiflayim — 'double twofold') — an intensified doubling unique to Hebrew, echoing Isaiah 40:2 (כִּי לָקְחָה מִיַּד יהוה כִּפְלַיִם — 'she has received from YHWH's hand double') and Jeremiah 16:18 (וְשִׁלַּמְתִּי... מִשְׁנֶה — 'I will repay double'). The Hebrew uses an emphatic cognate intensification (כפל כפלים) that has no equivalent in Greek's simple διπλώσατε ('double').

Uses שַׁלֵּם (shalem, H7999 — 'repay/complete') — from the root of shalom. This is covenantal restitution language — restoring balance through just recompense (Ex 21:34,36, 22:1-14). Greek ἀπόδοτε ('give back') is simpler.
greek_deviations: Greek adds a whole clause about the cup: 'in the cup which she mixed, mix for her double' (ἐν τῷ ποτηρίῳ ᾧ ἐκέρασε, κεράσατε αὐτῇ διπλοῦν) — absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:2 — 'Speak tenderly to Jerusalem... that she has received from YHWH's hand double (kiflayim) for all her sins.' The same doubling language applied to Jerusalem's punishment is now applied to Babylon.

verses.translation: And as she was haughty{H1342} and went{H1980} after{H310} her lusts{H8378}, thus do{H6213} to her afflictions; for she thinks{H2803} in her heart{H3820}: I am a queen{H4436} and I shall not be{H1961} a widow{H490}, and no distress shall I see{H7200}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 47:8: אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד לֹא אֵשֵׁב אַלְמָנָה ('I am, and there is none besides me; I shall not sit as a widow'). The Hebrew preserves the Isaiah 47 prophecy against Babylon — the woman speaks Babylon's own words. Greek κάθημαι βασίλισσα ('I sit as queen') approximates but does not preserve the Isaiah verbal form.

Uses הִתְגָּאָה (hitga'ah — 'was haughty/exalted herself', from ga'ah H1342). This is the verb YHWH uses for his own exaltation (Ex 15:1,21 — 'for he has triumphed gloriously/exalted himself greatly' — גָּאֹה גָּאָה). The harlot commits the sin of usurping divine exaltation. Greek ἐδόξασεν ἑαυτήν ('glorified herself') misses this specific OT echo.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'was haughty' (divine exaltation verb). Greek: 'glorified herself.' Different concept.
Hebrew: 'went after her lusts.' Greek: 'lived luxuriously' (ἐστρηνίασε). Hebrew emphasizes pursuit of desire; Greek emphasizes lifestyle.
translation_notes: עִינּוּיִם (innuyim — 'afflictions') is a post-biblical Hebrew form from the root ענה (anah — 'to afflict'). No standard Strong's number.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress') is a later Hebrew form. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Isaiah 47:7-8 — 'You said, I shall be a lady forever... I shall not sit as a widow (לא אשב אלמנה) nor know the loss of children.' Babylon's self-description is Isaiah's prophecy being fulfilled.

verses.translation: And because of this her sorrows shall come{H935} in one{H259} day{H3117}: the death{H4194} and the sorrow and the famine{H7458}; and with fire{H784} she shall be burned{H8313}; for mighty{H6099} is the Lord{H113} YHWH{H3068} who judges{H8199} her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the combined title הָאָדוֹן יַהְוֶה (ha-Adon YHWH — 'the Lord YHWH') — a distinctly OT divine title (Isa 3:1, 10:33, Mic 4:13 etc.). Greek: Κύριος ὁ Θεός ('Lord God'). A back-translator from Greek would write אדני אלהים (Adonai Elohim — 'Lord God'), not the specific Adon + YHWH combination.

Uses עָצוּם (atsum, H6099 — 'mighty/powerful') — used in the OT for overwhelming military power and numerical might (Num 22:6, Deut 4:38, 9:1, 26:5, Joel 2:2, Isa 53:12). Greek ἰσχυρός ('strong') is more generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Lord YHWH.' Greek: 'Lord God.' Different divine title.
Hebrew: 'mighty' (atsum — military/overwhelming). Greek: 'strong' (ischyros — general).
textual_notes: Isaiah 47:9 — 'These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day (ביום אחד): the loss of children and widowhood.' The 'in one day' formula is from Isaiah's Babylon oracle.

verses.translation: And the kings{H4428} of the earth{H776} who committed fornication{H2184} with her shall be desolate{H8074} over her, when they see{H7200} the smoke{H6227} from the fire{H784}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שָׁמְמוּ (shamemu — 'shall be desolate/appalled', from shamem H8074). This is the same root as שְׁמָמָה (shemamah — 'desolation') from 17:16. Greek κόψονται ('shall beat their breasts/wail') is a mourning action. Hebrew: they become DESOLATE (they share in the devastation); Greek: they WAIL (they mourn externally). A back-translator from Greek 'wail' would use ספדו (safdu — 'lament') or קוננו (qonenu — 'wail'), not the desolation verb shamem.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall be desolate' (shamem — share in devastation). Greek: 'shall weep and wail' (κλαύσουσι καὶ κόψονται — mourning actions). Different response.
Greek adds 'and wail' (κόψονται) and 'when they see the smoke of her burning (τοῦ πυρώσεως αὐτῆς).' Hebrew is more concise.

verses.translation: And they shall stand{H5975} from afar{H7350} because of dread{H367}, and shall say{H559}: Woe{H188}, alas, the great{H1419} city{H5892} Bavel{H894}! Suddenly{H6597} your breaking{H7667} has come{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אֵימָה (eimah, H367 — 'dread/terror') — the word for paralyzing fear used in the Exodus narrative (Ex 15:16 — 'terror and dread shall fall upon them') and the covenant curses (Deut 32:25). Greek φόβος ('fear') is generic. A back-translator from Greek 'fear' would use יראה (yirah — 'fear'), not the Exodus-terror word eimah.

Uses שְׁבוּרָתַיִךְ (shevuratayikh — 'your breaking') — related to שֶׁבֶר (shever, H7667 — 'breaking/fracture/destruction'). This echoes Jeremiah's constant refrain about שֶׁבֶר (Jer 4:6,20, 6:1,14, 8:21, 14:17, 48:3,5, 50:22,46, 51:54). Greek: ἡ κρίσις σου ('your judgment'). Hebrew: BREAKING (physical/structural destruction); Greek: JUDGMENT (legal verdict). A back-translator from 'judgment' would write משפטך (mishpatekh), not shevurah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your breaking' (structural destruction). Greek: 'your judgment' (legal verdict).
Hebrew: 'because of dread' (eimah). Greek: 'for fear of her torment' (expanded).
Greek: 'in one hour' (ἐν μιᾷ ὥρᾳ). Hebrew: 'suddenly' (פתאם). Different temporal markers.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 50:46 — 'At the cry, The breaking (שבר) of Babylon, the earth trembles.' The exact vocabulary of Babylon's שבר.

verses.translation: And the merchants{H5503} shall weep{H1058} and hiss{H8319} at you, because no one shall buy{H7069} any merchandise from them anymore{H5750}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שָׁרְקוּ (sharqu — 'hiss/whistle', from sharaq H8319) — the OT gesture of horror and contempt at a destroyed place (1 Ki 9:8, Jer 19:8, 49:17, 50:13, Lam 2:15-16, Mic 6:16, Zeph 2:15). Greek πενθοῦσιν ('mourn'). COMPLETELY different: Hebrew — hissing in horror/contempt (a physical reaction of shock); Greek — mourning in grief. A back-translator from Greek 'mourn' would use ספדו (safdu — 'lament') or התאבלו (hit'ablu — 'mourned'), not the hissing verb sharaq.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'weep and hiss' (grief + horror). Greek: 'weep and mourn' (grief + grief). Hebrew has the OT destruction-hissing gesture.
translation_notes: 'Hiss' for sharaq — the Hebrew gesture of drawing breath sharply through the teeth in shock, used when viewing ruins.
textual_notes: Lamentations 2:15 — 'All who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss (שרקו) and wag their heads.' The identical verb for reaction to Jerusalem's destruction.

verses.translation: The merchandise of gold{H2091} and silver{H3701} and goodly{H2896} stones{H68} and pearls and silk and all{H3605} kinds of woods{H6086} and kinds of vessels{H3627} of silver{H3701} and iron{H1270} and tin{H913} and lead{H5777}.

one_way_hebrew: The metal list בַּרְזֶל וּבְדִיל וְעוֹפֶרֶת ('iron and tin and lead') echoes Ezekiel 27:12 where Tarshish trades with Tyre in 'silver, iron, tin, and lead' (כסף ברזל בדיל ועופרת). The Hebrew author uses the Ezekiel 27 trade-list vocabulary. Greek lists different items in different order.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list is more condensed. Greek adds: 'purple, scarlet, fine linen,' various types of wood (thyine), 'ivory,' 'marble,' and 'brass' — items absent from the Hebrew list. The lists diverge significantly.
translation_notes: 'Goodly stones' (אבנים טובים) — again the OT standard rather than 'precious stones.'
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:12-25 provides the comprehensive trade list for Tyre that the Hebrew Revelation draws upon for Babylon's merchandise.

verses.translation: And wine{H3196} and oil{H8081} and white{H3836} bread{H3899} and wheat{H2406}, and cattle{H1241} and lambs{H3532}, and horses{H5483} and wagons{H5699}, and souls{H5315} of man{H120}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נִשְׁמוֹת אָדָם (nishmot adam — 'souls of man') — the EXACT phrase from Ezekiel 27:13 where Tyre trades in נֶפֶשׁ אָדָם (nefesh adam — 'souls of man'). Hebrew uses נשמות (nishmot — 'souls/breaths') from the creation word נשמה (neshamah — Gen 2:7, 'breath of life'). Greek: σωμάτων καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνθρώπων ('bodies and souls of men'). Greek adds 'bodies' (σωμάτων) which is absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew sees only SOULS being traded; the Greek adds the physical body.
Uses עֲגָלִים (agalim — 'wagons/carts', H5699). Greek ῥεδῶν ('chariots/carriages') is a Latin loanword (rheda). The Hebrew uses the native OT word for carts (Gen 45:19,21,27, Num 7:3-8).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'souls of man.' Greek: 'bodies and souls of men.' Greek adds 'bodies.'
Hebrew: 'white bread.' Greek: σεμίδαλιν ('fine flour'). Different commodity.
Hebrew: 'wagons.' Greek: 'chariots' (ῥεδῶν — Latin loanword).
translation_notes: 'Souls of man' — the trade in human beings, the ultimate moral degradation. The Hebrew uses the creation-breath word (neshamah) to describe the commodity.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:13 — 'Javan, Tubal, and Meshech traded with you; they exchanged souls of man (נפש אדם) and vessels of bronze for your merchandise.' The slave trade vocabulary is drawn from Ezekiel.

verses.translation: And the fruits that were a satisfaction{H5183} of spirit{H7307} for you have gone{H1980} from you, and all{H3605} the esteemed things have gone{H1980}, and you shall find{H4672} them no more{H5750}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נַחַת רוּחַ (nachat ruach — 'satisfaction of spirit') — a distinctly Hebrew/rabbinic phrase meaning inner pleasure or spiritual contentment (Eccl 4:6, 6:5; common in Mishnaic Hebrew). Greek ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῆς ψυχῆς ('the desire of the soul') is different — unfulfilled desire vs. achieved contentment. A back-translator from Greek 'desire' would use תאוה (ta'avah — 'desire'), not the rabbinic nachat ruach.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'satisfaction of spirit' (achieved contentment). Greek: 'desire of the soul' (unfulfilled desire). Opposite orientation.
Hebrew: 'esteemed things' (חשובים). Greek: 'luxurious and splendid things' (τὰ λιπαρὰ καὶ τὰ λαμπρά).

verses.translation: And the merchants{H5503} who sold{H4376} her these things{H1697} shall stand{H5975} from afar{H7350} and shall weep{H1058} over her.

greek_deviations: Greek adds mourning details: 'weeping and mourning' (κλαίοντες καὶ πενθοῦντες). Hebrew has only 'weep.'

verses.translation: And they shall say{H559}: Woe{H188}, alas, the great{H1419} city{H5892} Bavel{H894}, which was clothed{H3847} in silk{H4897} and in gold{H2091} and in goodly{H2896} stones{H68} and pearls.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'silk and gold and goodly stones and pearls.' Greek: 'fine linen and purple and scarlet (βύσσινον καὶ πορφυροῦν καὶ κόκκινον) and... gold and precious stone and pearls.' Greek has three fabric types; Hebrew has one (silk).

verses.translation: For in one{H259} hour all{H3605} was destroyed{H2717}: your traders, your sailors{H4419} and your shipmen{H2259}, repairers of your breaches and merchants of your wares, and all{H3605} your men{H582} of war{H4421} shall stand{H5975} from afar{H7350}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — DIRECT EZEKIEL 27 VOCABULARY: This verse uses FIVE specific nautical/trade terms from Ezekiel 27's prophecy against Tyre: (1) מַלָּחַיִךְ (mallachayikh — 'your sailors', H4419, Ezek 27:9,27,29); (2) חֹבְלָיִךְ (chovlayikh — 'your shipmen/pilots', H2259, Ezek 27:8,27,28,29); (3) מַחֲזִיקֵי בִדְקֵךְ (machazikei bidqekh — 'repairers of your breaches', Ezek 27:9,27 — בדק = breach/crack in a ship); (4) עֹרְבֵי מַעֲרָבֵךְ (orvei ma'aravekh — 'merchants of your wares', Ezek 27:27 — ערב = exchange/guarantee/trade); (5) אַנְשֵׁי מִלְחַמְתֵּךְ (anshei milchamtekh — 'your men of war', Ezek 27:27). This is virtually a quotation of Ezekiel 27:27. Greek uses generic nautical terms (κυβερνήτης, ναῦται etc.). No back-translator from Greek would independently reconstruct the specific Ezekiel 27 terminology.

Uses נֶחֱרַב (necherav — 'was destroyed/laid waste', from charav H2717) — the verb for the destruction of cities and the Temple (Isa 60:12, Jer 26:9, Ezek 26:19). The root חרב also produces חורבן (churban — 'destruction'), the standard term for the Temple's destruction.
greek_deviations: Hebrew preserves five Ezekiel 27 nautical terms. Greek uses standard Greek maritime vocabulary. The lists do not correspond 1:1.
Hebrew: 'repairers of your breaches' (ship repair). Greek: no equivalent — this specialized term is absent.
translation_notes: בֶּדֶק (bedeq, H919) — 'breach/crack' — specifically of ship damage (2 Ki 12:5-12, Ezek 27:9,27). The word is also used for Temple repairs.
The entire verse reads as a list from Ezekiel 27:27, applied to Babylon instead of Tyre — the Hebrew author sees the two prophetic destructions as parallel.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:27 — 'Your riches, your wares, your merchandise (מערבך), your sailors (מלחיך), your shipmen (חבליך), the repairers of your breaches (מחזיקי בדקך), the dealers in your merchandise, and all your men of war (כל אנשי מלחמתך)... shall sink into the heart of the seas.' Nearly verbatim.

verses.translation: [...] And they cry out{H6817} at the time they saw{H7200} the smoke{H6227}, saying{H559}: Who{H4310} is comparable{H1819} to the great{H1419} city{H5892}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses נִדְמָה (nidmah — 'is comparable/is like', from damah H1819 — 'to resemble/be like'). This echoes the mockery of Tyre in Ezekiel 27:32 — מִי כְצוֹר כְּדֻמָּה ('who is like Tyre, like the silenced one'). Greek: τίς ὁμοία τῇ πόλει τῇ μεγάλῃ ('who is like the great city'). While similar, the Hebrew nidmah connects to the Ezekiel/Tyre pattern; the Greek approximates but loses the specific verbal form.
greek_deviations: The Hebrew manuscript has a lacuna (gap) at the start of this verse, marked by [      ].
textual_notes: Ezekiel 27:32 — 'Who is like Tyre, like the silenced one in the midst of the sea?' The same question of incomparability.

verses.translation: And they shall cast{H2236} dust{H6083} upon their heads{H7218}, crying out{H6817} and weeping{H1058} and mourning{H56} and saying{H559}: Woe{H188}, woe{H188} to the great{H1419} city{H5892} Bavel{H894}, for from her all{H3605} the merchants{H5503} who had ships{H591} in the sea{H3220} grew rich from her merchandise, and now in one{H259} hour all{H3605} was destroyed{H2717}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יִזְרְקוּ עָפָר עַל רָאשֵׁיהֶם ('they shall cast dust upon their heads') — the specific OT mourning ritual using the verb זָרַק (zaraq, H2236 — 'to hurl/fling'). This is the priest's verb for hurling blood against the altar (Ex 24:6, Lev 1:5,11, Num 18:17). Using the priestly hurling-verb for the mourning gesture adds ritual gravity. Greek ἔβαλον χοῦν ('threw dust') uses the generic 'throw.'
translation_notes: עַכְשָׁיו (akhshav — 'now') is standard later Hebrew, absent from biblical Hebrew.
textual_notes: Job 2:12 — 'they sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven.' Lamentations 2:10 — 'they have cast dust upon their heads.' The dust-on-heads mourning ritual.

verses.translation: Rejoice{H8055}, O heavens{H8064}, and his holy ones{H6918} and his prophets{H5030}, for YHWH{H3068} has avenged{H5358} their vengeance{H5360} upon her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses a COGNATE ACCUSATIVE: נִקַּם אֶת נִקְמָתֵיהֶם (niqqam et niqmateihem — 'avenged their vengeance') — a classic Hebrew intensifying construction where the verb and its object share the same root (nqm). This idiomatic Hebrew pattern (cf. Gen 40:8 — חלמנו חלום, 'we dreamed a dream'; Num 11:4 — התאוו תאוה, 'they desired a desire') is natural in Hebrew composition. Greek ἔκρινεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ κρίμα ὑμῶν ('God judged your judgment') uses JUDGMENT vocabulary, not vengeance. Hebrew: VENGEANCE (naqam); Greek: JUDGMENT (krima). Entirely different legal framework — blood vengeance vs. judicial verdict.
YHWH again (H3068) vs. Greek Θεός.

תִּשְׂמְחוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם ('Rejoice, O heavens') echoes Deuteronomy 32:43 (הַרְנִינוּ גוֹיִם עַמּוֹ) and Psalm 96:11 (יִשְׂמְחוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם — 'let the heavens rejoice'). The Hebrew command to the heavens to rejoice is standard OT praise language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'avenged their vengeance' (blood vengeance). Greek: 'judged your judgment' (judicial verdict). Different legal concept.
Hebrew: YHWH. Greek: God.
Hebrew: 'his holy ones and his prophets.' Greek: 'holy apostles and prophets.' Greek adds 'apostles' where Hebrew has 'his holy ones.'
translation_notes: 'Avenged their vengeance' — the cognate accusative construction emphasizes the completeness and appropriateness of the retribution.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:43 — 'Rejoice, O nations, his people, for he will avenge (ינקם) the blood of his servants, and he will render vengeance (נקם) to his adversaries.' The exact vocabulary of divine vengeance.

verses.translation: And one{H259} messenger{H4397} took{H3947} a great{H1419} stone{H68} like a millstone{H7347} and cast{H2236} it into the sea{H3220}, and said{H559}: Thus shall Bavel{H894} sink{H8257} and shall not rise{H6965} again{H5750}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — DIRECT ALLUSION to Jeremiah 51:63-64: Jeremiah commands Seraiah to bind a stone to the scroll of prophecy against Babylon and cast it into the Euphrates, saying כָּכָה תִּשְׁקַע בָּבֶל ('thus shall Babylon SINK'). The Hebrew Revelation uses the EXACT verb תִּשְׁקַע (tishqa — 'shall sink', from shaqa H8257) and the same formula כָּכָה תשׁקע בבל. Greek uses βληθήσεται ('shall be thrown') — different verb. A back-translator from Greek's 'thrown' would use תושלך (tushlakh — 'shall be thrown'), NOT the specific Jeremiah שקע (sink).
The verb pair תִּשְׁקַע... תָקוּם (tishqa... taqum — 'sink... rise') echoes Jeremiah 51:64 exactly: 'Thus shall Babylon sink and NOT RISE (ולא תקום).' Both verbs match Jeremiah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall sink' (שקע — specific sinking verb from Jeremiah). Greek: 'shall be thrown down' (βληθήσεται — general throwing). Different action.
Greek adds 'with violence' (ὁρμήματι) — absent from Hebrew.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:63-64 — 'When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates and say: Thus shall Babylon sink (ככה תשקע בבל) and shall not rise (ולא תקום).' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Jeremiah's enacted prophecy.

verses.translation: And no longer shall be heard{H8085} in her the voice{H6963} of joy{H8342} and the voice{H6963} of gladness{H8057}, the voice{H6963} of the bridegroom{H2860} and the voice{H6963} of the bride{H3618}; nor any tool{H3627} of craft{H4399} from the masters{H1167} of crafts{H4399}; and the sound{H6963} of the millstones{H7347} shall no longer be heard{H8085} in you.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VERBATIM JEREMIAH QUOTATION: קוֹל שָׂשׂוֹן וְקוֹל שִׂמְחָה קוֹל חָתָן וְקוֹל כַּלָּה ('the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride') is an EXACT quote from Jeremiah 7:34, 16:9, 25:10, and 33:11. This four-fold formula is unique to Jeremiah — it appears NOWHERE else in the OT. The Hebrew Revelation reproduces it verbatim. Greek approximates but rearranges: it adds 'voice of harpers and musicians and pipers and trumpeters' (φωνὴ κιθαρῳδῶν καὶ μουσικῶν καὶ αὐλητῶν καὶ σαλπιστῶν) BEFORE the bridegroom/bride — which breaks the Jeremiah formula. A back-translator from Greek would not independently reconstruct the exact Jeremiah quote.

Also quotes Jeremiah 25:10 which adds קוֹל רֵחַיִם ('sound of millstones'). The Hebrew combines Jeremiah 7:34/16:9 (voice formula) with 25:10 (millstone sound) — a conflation natural for a Hebrew author steeped in Jeremiah.

Uses בַּעֲלֵי מְלָאכוֹת (ba'alei melakhot — 'masters of crafts', H1167 + H4399). בַּעַל (ba'al — 'master/owner/lord') is the OT word for the Canaanite deity, but in its primary sense means 'master/possessor.' The Hebrew compound 'masters of crafts' is an OT construction (1 Chr 4:14, Neh 11:35).
greek_deviations: Greek adds four types of musicians (harpers, musicians, pipers, trumpeters) before the bridegroom/bride — absent from Hebrew, and breaking the Jeremiah formula.
Hebrew switches from 3rd person 'in her' (בה) to 2nd person 'in you' (בך) within the same verse — a jarring but authentic shift that suggests direct prophetic address.
translation_notes: The four-fold 'voice of... voice of...' formula is preserved exactly as it appears in Jeremiah.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:10 — 'I will take from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones (קול רחים) and the light of the lamp.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces the Jeremiah passage with remarkable precision.

verses.translation: And no longer shall the light{H216} of the luminaries{H3974} shine{H2224}; for your merchants{H5503} were princes{H8269} upon the ground{H127}; for by{H3027} your sorceries{H3785} all{H3605} the peoples{H5971} were led astray{H5496}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְּאוֹרֹת (me'orot, H3974 — 'luminaries') — the Genesis 1:14-16 creation word, consistently used throughout this Hebrew text (ch. 21:11,23). The extinguishing of the luminaries is DE-CREATION — Babylon's fall undoes the creative act. Greek has simply 'light of a lamp' (φῶς λύχνου). The Hebrew scales up the imagery from a household lamp to the cosmic luminaries.
Again uses הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah, H127 — 'the ground'), not erets. Consistent ch. 18 pattern (vv. 1, 23, 24).

Uses שָׂרִים (sarim, H8269 — 'princes/officials') — the OT governmental term for rulers and commanders (Gen 12:15, Ex 1:11, 1 Sam 8:12, 1 Ki 4:2). Greek: μεγιστᾶνες ('great men'). Hebrew implies governmental authority; Greek implies social status.

Uses הִסִּיתוּ (hissitu — 'they incited/led astray', from sut H5496) — the verb used for inciting someone to evil, especially to idolatry (Deut 13:6 — 'if your brother entices you [יסיתך] to serve other gods'; 1 Ki 21:25 — Jezebel 'incited' Ahab; Job 2:3 — the adversary 'incited' God). Greek ἐπλανήθησαν ('were led astray') is passive. Hebrew: active incitement to evil; Greek: passive deception.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'light of the luminaries' (cosmic). Greek: 'light of a lamp' (domestic). Different scale.
Hebrew: 'princes upon the ground.' Greek: 'great men of the earth.'
Hebrew: 'by your sorceries they led astray' (active). Greek: 'by your sorcery were all nations deceived' (passive).
translation_notes: כִּשּׁוּפַיִךְ (kishufayikh — 'your sorceries', from kashaf H3784) — the Torah sorcery term (Ex 7:11, 22:18 — 'you shall not permit a sorceress to live'). Greek: φαρμακεία ('pharmacy/sorcery') — potion/drug-based magic.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:10 also includes 'and the light of the lamp' (ואור הנר) among the sounds/sights that will cease. The Hebrew continues the Jeremiah 25 series.
Nahum 3:4 — 'Because of the many harlotries of the harlot... who sells nations by her harlotries and peoples by her sorceries (בכשפיה).' Same vocabulary.

verses.translation: And in her was found{H4672} the blood{H1818} of the holy ones{H6918} and prophets{H5030}, and of all{H3605} those who were slain{H2026} upon the ground{H127}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נֶהֶרְגוּ (nehergu — 'were slain', from harag H2026) — the OT violence verb for killing (Gen 4:8 — Cain KILLED Abel; Ex 2:14, 32:27). Greek ἐσφαγμένων ('slaughtered') is from σφάζω, which can imply ritual/sacrificial slaughter. The Hebrew uses the common murder verb, not sacrificial language.

Again הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adamah — 'the ground', H127) — consistent throughout ch. 18. This echoes Genesis 4:10 — 'the voice of your brother's blood cries to me FROM THE GROUND (מן האדמה).' The blood of the slain cries from the adamah, just as Abel's blood cried from the adamah. A back-translator from Greek γῆ would use ארץ, not create this Genesis 4 echo.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'upon the ground' (adamah — Genesis echo). Greek: 'upon the earth' (γῆ — generic).
textual_notes: Genesis 4:10 — 'The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground (מן האדמה).' The blood-on-the-adamah motif links Babylon's bloodguilt to the primal murder.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 18 is saturated with direct OT quotations, most prominently from Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The most striking one-way markers are: (1) The VERBATIM Jeremiah quotation of the four-fold voice formula (קול ששון וקול שמחה קול חתן וקול כלה — Jer 7:34/16:9/25:10); (2) The VERBATIM Jeremiah 51:63-64 sinking formula (ככה תשקע בבל ולא תקום); (3) FIVE specific Ezekiel 27 nautical/trade terms in v17 (mallachim, chovlim, machazikei bedeq, orvei ma'arav, anshei milchamah) that match the Tyre destruction prophecy; (4) Consistent use of אדמה ('ground') instead of ארץ ('earth') throughout the chapter, echoing Genesis creation language and Gen 4:10; (5) שטנים ('adversaries') vs. Greek 'demons'; (6) The cognate accusative נקם את נקמתם ('avenged their vengeance'); (7) YHWH used where Greek has Θεός; (8) מאורות (Genesis creation 'luminaries') vs. Greek 'lamp'; (9) The Isaiah 47:8 queen/widow self-declaration. The chapter reads as an extended midrash on Jeremiah 25, 50-51 and Ezekiel 27, applied to eschatological Babylon.
